title: People
goal: Introduce yourself and your family, and ask people their name, where they're from and what they do.

notes.h: I, you, he, she, and 哋 for plurals
notes.p: {{我|ngo5}} = I / me, {{你|nei5}} = you, {{佢|keoi5}} = he, she or it (one word for all three). Add {{哋|dei6}} to make any of them plural: {{我哋|ngo5 dei6}} we, {{你哋|nei5 dei6}} you all, {{佢哋|keoi5 dei6}} they. Pronouns never change form, so "me" is also {{我|ngo5}}. Many Hong Kongers say {{你|nei5}} with an l sound (lei5) and drop the ng of {{我|ngo5}}; both are fine.
ex: He's a doctor. / She's a doctor.
keoi5 dei6 hai6 ngo5 pang4 jau5
ngo5 dei6 zyu6 hai2 zi1 gaa1 go1

notes.h: 係 "is", 叫 "is called", 喺 "is at"
notes.p: {{係|hai6}} (low, level) links two things: I am a doctor, this is my wife. {{叫|giu3}} gives a name. {{喺|hai2}} (rising) means "at / in" a place, and on its own it already means "is at": {{我媽媽喺香港|ngo5 maa4 maa1 hai2 hoeng1 gong2}} = my mom is in Hong Kong. Never put {{係|hai6}} in front of a place to say where someone is. Listen for the tone: hai6 stays low, hai2 rises.

notes.h: 嘅 for 's, and when to drop it
notes.p: {{嘅|ge3}} works like English 's: {{Wing嘅家姐|Wing ge3 gaa1 ze1}} = Wing's older sister. After a pronoun, people usually drop it for family and close friends: {{我老婆|ngo5 lou5 po4}} = my wife, {{我媽媽|ngo5 maa4 maa1}} = my mom. To introduce someone, point with {{呢個|ni1 go3}} (this) or {{嗰個|go2 go3}} (that): {{呢個係我老婆|ni1 go3 hai6 ngo5 lou5 po4}}.
ex: ni1 go3 hai6 ngo5 lou5 po4
go2 go3 hai6 ngo5 go4 go1

notes.h: Question words stay where the answer goes
notes.p: Cantonese doesn't move question words to the front. Put the question word where the answer will go: {{你叫咩名呀？|nei5 giu3 me1 meng2 aa3}} (you are called what name?) is answered {{我叫Dan|ngo5 giu3 Dan}}. {{咩|me1}} = what, {{邊個|bin1 go3}} = who, {{邊度|bin1 dou6}} = where, {{點|dim2}} = how. Adding {{呀|aa3}} at the end makes a question softer and friendlier. Note that {{名|meng2}} is said meng2 in speech.
ex: nei5 zyu6 hai2 bin1 dou6 aa3

notes.p: {{呢|ni1}} (this) is high and flat; the same character as a question particle, {{你呢？|nei5 ne1}} (and you?), is ne1. {{嗰|go2}} (that) rises. In {{男人|naam4 jan2}} and {{女人|neoi5 jan2}} the last syllable rises to jan2, but in {{美國人|mei5 gwok3 jan4}} it stays low: jan4.

roleplay.title: Meeting someone at a party
roleplay.setup: You're at a friend's party in Hong Kong and someone you don't know comes over to say hello. Introduce yourself and find out about them.
roleplay.persona: You are Wing, a friendly Hong Konger in your thirties who works as a teacher and lives in Sha Tin with your husband and your older sister. Speak simple colloquial Hong Kong Cantonese using mostly words from levels 1 and 2: 你好, 叫, 係, 喺, 住, 邊度, 咩, 邊個, 點, 呀, family words (老公, 家姐, 爸爸, 媽媽). Use short sentences. Ask the learner's name, where they are from, where they live and what they do for work, and answer their questions about you. If they ask you to repeat or slow down, do it.
opening: nei5 hou2! ngo5 giu3 Wing. nei5 giu3 me1 meng2 aa3
roleplay.opening_en: Hi! I'm Wing. What's your name?
goals: Say where you're from and where you live
Say what you do for work
Ask her one question about her family

roleplay.title: Showing family photos
roleplay.setup: A friendly older neighbour wants to see the photos on your phone. Tell her who each person is and where they are.
roleplay.persona: You are Auntie Wong, a chatty retired Hong Kong woman. Speak simple colloquial Hong Kong Cantonese using mostly words from levels 1 and 2. Point at imaginary photos and ask short questions like 呢個係邊個呀？, 嗰個男人呢？, 佢喺邊度呀？, 佢係邊度人呀？, 佢做咩工㗎？. React warmly to the answers and gently model the right word if the learner mixes up 係 (is) and 喺 (is at), or 呢個 (this) and 嗰個 (that).
opening: ni1 go3 hai6 bin1 go3 aa3
goals: Say who someone in a photo is
